props.title: An

sections.content: An marks a gorgeous meditation on food, friendship and forgiveness from Japanese director Naomi Kawase. The film centers on Sentaro, a dorayaki shop owner, and Tokue, an elderly woman whose perfect sweet bean paste recipe transforms both his business and their lives. Like Kawase's other works including Sweet Bean (2015) and Still the Water (2014), An uses food preparation as a lens to explore deeper themes of social prejudice, personal redemption and finding meaning through craft. The methodical scenes of cooking dorayaki connect to Japan's appreciation for shokunin (artisan) culture, similar to Jiro Dreams of Sushi (2011).

sections.content: The film's gentle pacing and attention to natural beauty align with other contemplative Japanese dramas like Nobody Knows (2004) and Our Little Sister (2015). Kawase's signature documentary-influenced style captures intimate moments of food preparation with almost religious reverence. The handling of social discrimination against Hansen's disease (leprosy) patients connects to broader Japanese films addressing societal outcasts, like Departures (2008) and Like Father, Like Son (2013).

While food films often focus on haute cuisine or restaurant drama (Burnt (2015), Ratatouille (2007)), An celebrates humble street food and traditional recipes passed between generations. This connects it to other Asian films exploring food's role in cultural preservation like Eat Drink Man Woman (1994) and The Lunchbox (2013). The film's exploration of mentorship through cooking recalls East Side Sushi (2014). SUBHEAD: Food as Memory and Healing

sections.content: The film's treatment of food as memory carrier and healing agent connects to a rich tradition of culinary cinema. Like Like Water for Chocolate (1992) and Julie & Julia (2009), An shows how recipes preserve cultural memory and personal history. The attention to traditional Japanese sweets parallels other films celebrating specific food traditions, such as City of Gold (2015) and For Grace (2015).
